title: Adaptive load-probe harness for cascading batching and queueing effects
creator: Liam Chen
description: Build an automated, reproducible load-probing harness that reveals how continuous batching interacts with queueing under mixed request mixes (short chat prompts, long-form generation, and embedding requests). The goal is to quantify tokens/sec, per-request p95, and CPU/GPU utilization as arrival rate, priority queuing, and batching windows change. This ticket covers design of the probe patterns, implementation of adaptive arrival generators, metric collection and baseline regression detection logic.
test_plan: 1) Implement three synthetic arrival classes: interactive (1-32 tokens, 50-200ms think time), long-gen (512-2048 tokens, sustained streaming), embedding (single-call, fixed tokens). 2) Create adaptive driver that varies offered load in phases (ramp, plateau, spike, decay) and toggles batching window (1ms, 8ms, 32ms) and queue admission policy (FIFO, priority). 3) Capture per-request latency, p95/p99, tokens/sec, queue length distribution, batch sizes, KV cache hit ratio, and GPU kernel utilization. 4) Feed metrics into regression detector with baseline from runtime-1.20. 5) Run 50+ experiments across model variants and seed with deterministic RNG for reproducibility.
updates: 2026-03-02: PoC driver implemented to emit mixed arrivals; validated simple FIFO case on local harness.
2026-03-04: Added metrics exporter for batch_size histogram and per-request queue_wait_ms; integrated with Prometheus test stack.
2026-03-06: Discovered that increasing batching window from 8ms -> 32ms raises tokens/sec ~18% for long-gen but increases p95 for interactive class by ~42% in FIFO. Logged trade-off for SLO configs.
2026-03-08: Implemented adaptive probe that performs binary search on offered load to find knee point for throughput without p95 regressions; initial runs stable on small cluster.
2026-03-10: Hooked regression detector with baseline snapshots and alert rules; opened PR for review (see links).
decisions: Use mixed-class arrival generator rather than replaying production traces to isolate batching/queueing variables.
Adopt latency-first SLO for interactive class (p95 <= 120ms) and throughput-first for long-gen (tokens/sec target per GPU).
Prioritize determinism: seed driver RNG and snapshot kernel versions to make runs comparable across days.
results_summary: Early experiments (runtime-1.20 baseline) show: 1) Small batching windows (1-4ms) maintain interactive p95 but underutilize GPUs, throughput low. 2) Medium windows (8ms) provide best overall cost/latency trade-off for mixed 70/20/10 workload. 3) Large windows (32ms) improve tokens/sec for long-gen by ~25% but cause interactive p95 regressions in high arrival-rate conditions. The adaptive knee-finder reduced operator guesswork and produced stable knee values within 10% across repeated runs. Regression detector flagged a kernel scheduling change in runtime-1.21 that increased interactive p95 by +18% under priority queueing; investigation assigned to ENG-18801.
